statement: Let \(q=p^a\) be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be a prime, put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\), and let \(X\) be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension \(d\ge1\) over \(\mathbb F_q\). Let \(Z\in\mathrm{CH}^d(X\times_{\mathbb F_q}X)_{\mathbb Q}\) be a correspondence such that \(\int_{X\times X}\mathrm{cl}(Z)\cup(\mathrm{cl}(A)\times \mathrm{cl}(B))=0\) in \(\mathbb Q_\ell\) for every \(i\ge0\) and all \(A\in\mathrm{CH}^i(X)_{\mathbb Q}\), \(B\in\mathrm{CH}^{d-i}(X)_{\mathbb Q}\). Then the endomorphism \(Z_*:\alpha\mapsto \mathrm{pr}_{2*}(\mathrm{pr}_1^*\alpha\cup \mathrm{cl}(Z))\) of \(\bigoplus_{n\ge0}H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is zero on \(H^0_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\oplus H^{2d}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\).
proof:
Proof. Throughout, k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q and \ell \neq p. Fix once and for all a nonzero element of \mathbb Q_\ell(1) and use it to identify \mathbb Q_\ell(n) with \mathbb Q_\ell for every n \in \mathbb Z; all cycle classes and cohomology classes are transported to \mathbb Q_\ell-valued classes by this identification, and all traces below are \mathbb Q_\ell-valued.

(0) Traces, pairings, and Gysin pushforwards.

(a) Trace on X. By lemma_77(a) applied with m = 1 and Y = X (pure dimension d \ge 1), there is a canonical isomorphism tr_X : H^{2d}_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \to \mathbb Q_\ell, normalized by tr_X(cl(x)) = [\kappa(x):\mathbb F_q] for every closed point x of X. In particular tr_X is injective.

(b) Trace on X \times X. The product X \times X = X \times_{\mathbb F_q} X is smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension 2d over \mathbb F_q. By lemma_77(a) applied with m = 1 and Y = X \times X, there is a canonical isomorphism tr_{X \times X} : H^{4d}_{\mathrm{et}}((X \times X)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \to \mathbb Q_\ell, normalized by tr_{X \times X}(cl(z)) = [\kappa(z):\mathbb F_q] for every closed point z of X \times X. For \omega \in H^{4d}_{\mathrm{et}}((X \times X)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) we write \int_{X \times X} \omega := tr_{X \times X}(\omega); this is the integral occurring in the hypothesis.

(c) Perfect pairings. By lemma_77(b) applied with m = 1, for Y \in \{X, X \times X\} of pure dimension e \in \{d, 2d\} and every n with 0 \le n \le 2e, the pairing H^n_{\mathrm{et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \times H^{2e-n}_{\mathrm{et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \to \mathbb Q_\ell, (a,b) \mapsto tr_Y(a \cup b), is perfect.

(d) Gysin pushforwards of the projections. Let pr_1, pr_2 : X \times X \to X be the two projections and pr_i^* the induced pullback on \ell-adic cohomology. For i \in \{1,2\} and each integer m, define pr_{i*} : H^{m+2d}_{\mathrm{et}}((X \times X)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \to H^m_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) to be the unique \mathbb Q_\ell-linear map such that

(\star)   tr_X(pr_{i*} a \cup b) = tr_{X \times X}(a \cup pr_i^* b)

for all a \in H^{m+2d}_{\mathrm{et}}((X \times X)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and all b \in H^{2d-m}_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). Existence and uniqueness: for fixed a, the assignment b \mapsto tr_{X \times X}(a \cup pr_i^* b) is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear functional on H^{2d-m}_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), and by (c) with Y = X and n = m the pairing H^m_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \times H^{2d-m}_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \to \mathbb Q_\ell is perfect; hence there is a unique element pr_{i*} a \in H^m_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) satisfying (\star) for all b. These are the Gysin pushforwards for the smooth projections that are used in lemma_483.

(e) Correspondences. Since dim(X \times X) = 2d and Z \in \mathrm{CH}^d(X \times_{\mathbb F_q} X)_{\mathbb Q}, the cycle class cl(Z) is an element of H^{2d}_{\mathrm{et}}((X \times X)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). For A \in \mathrm{CH}^i(X)_{\mathbb Q} and B \in \mathrm{CH}^{d-i}(X)_{\mathbb Q}, set cl(A) \times cl(B) := pr_1^* cl(A) \cup pr_2^* cl(B) \in H^{2d}_{\mathrm{et}}((X \times X)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). The hypothesis of the lemma then reads:

(H)   tr_{X \times X}(cl(Z) \cup (pr_1^* cl(A) \cup pr_2^* cl(B))) = 0 for every i \ge 0, every A \in \mathrm{CH}^i(X)_{\mathbb Q} and every B \in \mathrm{CH}^{d-i}(X)_{\mathbb Q}.

(f) The action of Z. For \alpha \in H^n_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) one has pr_1^* \alpha \in H^n_{\mathrm{et}}((X \times X)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), so pr_1^* \alpha \cup cl(Z) \in H^{n+2d}_{\mathrm{et}}((X \times X)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), and pr_{2*} maps this group to H^n_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). Hence Z_*(H^n_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)) \subseteq H^n_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell): Z_* preserves the cohomological degree, so the direct sum \bigoplus_{n \ge 0} H^n_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) is Z_*-stable with Z_* acting on each summand. Moreover X_k is connected because X is geometrically connected over \mathbb F_q, so H^0_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) = \mathbb Q_\ell \cdot 1, where 1 is the unit of the cohomology ring, i.e. the cycle class of the fundamental class [X] (the cycle class map is a ring homomorphism and sends [X] to 1).

(1) pr_{2*} cl(Z) = 0, hence Z_*(1) = 0.

Since pr_{2*} cl(Z) \in H^0_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) = \mathbb Q_\ell \cdot 1, write pr_{2*} cl(Z) = c \cdot 1 with c \in \mathbb Q_\ell. Let B \in \mathrm{CH}^d(X)_{\mathbb Q} be arbitrary, and apply (H) with i = 0 and A = [X] \in \mathrm{CH}^0(X)_{\mathbb Q}. Since cl([X]) = 1, we have cl(A) \times cl(B) = pr_1^* 1 \cup pr_2^* cl(B) = pr_2^* cl(B), so (H) gives tr_{X \times X}(cl(Z) \cup pr_2^* cl(B)) = 0. On the other hand, (\star) for pr_{2*} with m = 0, a = cl(Z) \in H^{2d}_{\mathrm{et}}((X \times X)_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and b = cl(B) \in H^{2d}_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) gives tr_X(pr_{2*} cl(Z) \cup cl(B)) = tr_{X \times X}(cl(Z) \cup pr_2^* cl(B)). Combining the two identities, tr_X(c \cdot 1 \cup cl(B)) = c \cdot tr_X(cl(B)) = 0 for every B \in \mathrm{CH}^d(X)_{\mathbb Q}.

Now choose a closed point x of X (such a point exists because X is a nonempty scheme of finite type over the finite field \mathbb F_q) and take B = [x] \in \mathrm{CH}^d(X)_{\mathbb Q}; a closed point of the d-dimensional variety X has codimension d. Then the normalization in (a) gives 0 = c \cdot tr_X(cl(x)) = c \cdot [\kappa(x):\mathbb F_q]. As [\kappa(x):\mathbb F_q] is a positive integer, it is nonzero in \mathbb Q_\ell, so c = 0. Hence pr_{2*} cl(Z) = 0. Consequently Z_*(1) = pr_{2*}(pr_1^* 1 \cup cl(Z)) = pr_{2*}(cl(Z)) = 0, i.e. Z_* vanishes on H^0_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

(2) pr_{1*} cl(Z) = 0.

The same argument with pr_1 and pr_2 interchanged, using the case i = d of (H). Write pr_{1*} cl(Z) = c' \cdot 1 with c' \in \mathbb Q_\ell. Let A \in \mathrm{CH}^d(X)_{\mathbb Q} and apply (H) with i = d and B = [X] \in \mathrm{CH}^0(X)_{\mathbb Q}. Since cl([X]) = 1, cl(A) \times cl(B) = pr_1^* cl(A) \cup pr_2^* 1 = pr_1^* cl(A), so (H) gives tr_{X \times X}(cl(Z) \cup pr_1^* cl(A)) = 0. By (\star) for pr_{1*} with m = 0, a = cl(Z) and b = cl(A), this says tr_X(pr_{1*} cl(Z) \cup cl(A)) = c' \cdot tr_X(cl(A)) = 0 for every A \in \mathrm{CH}^d(X)_{\mathbb Q}. Taking A = [x] for a closed point x gives c' \cdot [\kappa(x):\mathbb F_q] = 0, hence c' = 0. Thus pr_{1*} cl(Z) = 0.

(3) Z_* vanishes on H^{2d}_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

Let \alpha \in H^{2d}_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). Apply lemma_483 (whose hypotheses are exactly the present ones: q = p^a, \ell \neq p, X smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d \ge 1 over \mathbb F_q, k = \overline{\mathbb F}_q, the fixed identification \mathbb Q_\ell(1) \cong \mathbb Q_\ell, Z \in \mathrm{CH}^d(X \times_{\mathbb F_q} X)_{\mathbb Q}, and tr_X normalized as in (a)) with n = 2d, with this \alpha, and with \beta = 1 \in H^0_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) = H^{2d-2d}_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). It gives

tr_X(Z_*(\alpha) \cup 1) = tr_X(\alpha \cup Z^{\dagger}_*(1)),

where Z^{\dagger}_*(\beta) = pr_{1*}(pr_2^* \beta \cup cl(Z)). For \beta = 1 we have pr_2^* 1 = 1, hence Z^{\dagger}_*(1) = pr_{1*}(cl(Z)) = 0 by (2). Therefore tr_X(Z_*(\alpha)) = tr_X(\alpha \cup 0) = 0.

By (a), tr_X : H^{2d}_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \to \mathbb Q_\ell is an isomorphism, hence injective. So Z_*(\alpha) = 0. Since \alpha \in H^{2d}_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) was arbitrary, Z_* vanishes on H^{2d}_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell).

(4) Conclusion. By (f), Z_* preserves degrees, so Z_* acts on the direct sum \bigoplus_{n \ge 0} H^n_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) summand by summand. By (1) it acts as zero on the summand H^0_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), and by (3) as zero on the summand H^{2d}_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). Hence Z_* is zero on H^0_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) \oplus H^{2d}_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), as required. QED

Remark on the scope of the argument. The hypothesis (H) is used only in the two extreme cases i = 0 and i = d, which yield pr_{2*} cl(Z) = 0 and pr_{1*} cl(Z) = 0 respectively; the argument says nothing about the middle Kunneth component H^d \otimes H^d inside H^{2d}((X \times X)_k). In particular no nilpotence of Z_* is asserted or used, and cl(Z) is not assumed to vanish; this is consistent with the reviser's counterexample (an elliptic curve E with Z = [\Gamma_{[-1]}] - [\Delta], for which the hypothesis holds while Z_* = -2\,\mathrm{id} on H^1).

statement: Let K be a field of characteristic 0, let d≥0 be an integer, and let V=⊕_{n∈Z}V_n be a finite-dimensional Z-graded K-vector space with V_n=0 for n<0 and for n>2d. Let L∈End_K(V) satisfy L(V_n)⊆V_{n+2} for every n, and suppose that L^{d-n}:V_n→V_{2d-n} is an isomorphism for every 0≤n≤d. For 0≤r≤d put P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:V_r→V_{2d-r+2}), and set P^m=0 for m<0 and m>d. Then for every integer n with 0≤n≤2d the addition map ⊕_{k≥max(0,n-d)}P^{n-2k}→V_n, (x_k)_k↦Σ_k L^k x_k, is an isomorphism of K-vector spaces.
proof:
Let L^0=id. Recall that V_m=0 for m<0 and for m>2d, and P^m=0 for m<0 and for m>d. All direct sums below are finite because P^m vanishes outside 0≤m≤d. We prove that V_n is the indicated internal direct sum; this is exactly the assertion that the addition map is an isomorphism.

Step 1. For every 0≤m≤d, the map L^{d-m+1}:V_m→V_{2d-m+2} is surjective. If m=0, the target is V_{2d+2}=0; if m=1, the target is V_{2d+1}=0. If m≥2, take y∈V_{2d-m+2}. By the hypothesis applied to m-2, the map L^{d-m+2}:V_{m-2}→V_{2d-m+2} is an isomorphism. Choose x∈V_{m-2} with L^{d-m+2}x=y. Then Lx∈V_m and L^{d-m+1}(Lx)=y. Hence the map is surjective.

Step 2. For 0≤n≤d we have V_n=P^n⊕L(V_{n-2}), where V_{-2}=V_{-1}=0. For n=0,1, the target of L^{d-n+1}:V_n→V_{2d-n+2} is V_{2d+2} or V_{2d+1}, hence zero, so P^n=V_n, while L(V_{n-2})=0. For n≥2, let x∈V_n. By Step 1 with m=n, there exists y∈V_{n-2} such that L^{d-n+1}x=L^{d-n+2}y=L^{d-n+1}(Ly). Thus x-Ly∈P^n, so V_n=P^n+L(V_{n-2}). If p∈P^n∩L(V_{n-2}), write p=Ly with y∈V_{n-2}. Then 0=L^{d-n+1}p=L^{d-n+2}y. The hypothesis at n-2 says that L^{d-n+2}:V_{n-2}→V_{2d-n+2} is an isomorphism, so y=0 and p=0. Therefore the sum is direct.

Step 3. We prove by induction on n that for 0≤n≤d, V_n=⊕_{k≥0} L^k P^{n-2k}. For n=0, P^0=ker(L^{d+1}:V_0→V_{2d+2})=V_0, and all terms with k≥1 have negative upper index and vanish. For n=1, when d≥1, P^1=ker(L^d:V_1→V_{2d+1})=V_1, and again only k=0 contributes. For n≥2, Step 2 gives V_n=P^n⊕L(V_{n-2}). By induction, V_{n-2}=⊕_{k≥0}L^kP^{n-2-2k}. Also L is injective on V_{n-2}: if Lv=0, then L^{d-n+2}v=L^{d-n+1}(Lv)=0, and L^{d-n+2} is an isomorphism by the hypothesis at n-2. Hence L(V_{n-2})=⊕_{k≥0}L^{k+1}P^{n-2-2k}. Therefore V_n=P^n⊕⊕_{k≥1}L^kP^{n-2k}, which is the desired decomposition.

Step 4. Let d<n≤2d and put n'=2d-n, so 0≤n'<d. Step 3 gives V_{n'}=⊕_{k≥0}L^kP^{n'-2k}. The hypothesis applied to n' says that L^{n-d}=L^{d-n'}:V_{n'}→V_n is an isomorphism. An isomorphism carries a direct sum to the direct sum of the images, so V_n=⊕_{k≥0}L^{n-d+k}P^{n'-2k}. Setting j=n-d+k, the range is j≥n-d=max(0,n-d), and n'-2k=2d-n-2(j-n+d)=n-2j. Thus V_n=⊕_{j≥n-d}L^jP^{n-2j}. This is the required decomposition for n>d.

Steps 3 and 4 cover every integer n with 0≤n≤2d. Hence the addition map is an isomorphism in every degree.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let l != p be prime, let m>=1, and let k be an algebraic closure of F_q. Let X be smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension d>=1 over F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_l(1) and identify Tate twists with Q_l. Let xi be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor on X, let L be cup product with xi, and let F be the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius. Suppose L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_l)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_l) is an isomorphism for every 0<=n<=d. For 0<=r<=d put P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r_et(X_k,Q_l)->H^{2d-r+2}_et(X_k,Q_l)). Then F is diagonalizable over Qbar_l on H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) for every n>=0 if and only if F(P^r) is contained in P^r and F|_{P^r} is diagonalizable over Qbar_l for every 0<=r<=d.
proof:
DICTIONARY. For a finite-dimensional Q_l-vector space W and T in GL_{Q_l}(W), T is semisimple (i.e. W is a semisimple Q_l[T]-module) iff its minimal polynomial is squarefree iff that polynomial has distinct roots in the algebraic closure iff T tensor_{Q_l} Qbar_l is diagonalizable. Since char Q_l = 0, we use "semisimple" and "diagonalizable over Qbar_l" interchangeably, and may apply lemmas stated for semisimple operators to operators diagonalizable over Qbar_l.

STEP 0 (finiteness, vanishing, invertibility). Put V_n = H^n_et(X_k,Q_l) for n >= 0 and V_n = 0 for n < 0. (a) Each V_n is finite-dimensional: apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_45_finite_frob over the base field F_{q^m} (k is an algebraic closure of F_{q^m}, and X is proper over F_{q^m}) with K the constant sheaf Q_l on X_k carrying its natural q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism. (b) V_n = 0 for n > 2d: by Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing, since X_k is projective of pure dimension d over the algebraically closed field k and l != char(k) = p. (c) F lies in GL_{Q_l}(V_n) for every n: by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_6a with q^m in place of q. Consequently V = direct sum_{n in Z} V_n is finite-dimensional and Z-graded with V_n = 0 outside [0,2d].

STEP 1 (Frobenius-Lefschetz commutation and stability). Apply eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable with q^m in place of q (X smooth projective of pure dimension d over F_{q^m}; xi = cl(H) for the F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor H; L = cup product with xi): F circ L = q^m L circ F on every V_n, and for every 0 <= r <= d and every k >= 0 the subspaces P^r contained in V_r and L^k(P^r) contained in V_{r+2k} are stable under both F and F^{-1}. In particular the condition "F(P^r) contained in P^r" appearing in the statement is automatic.

STEP 2 (only if). Assume F is diagonalizable over Qbar_l on V_n for every n >= 0. Fix 0 <= r <= d. Since r <= d <= 2d, F|_{V_r} is diagonalizable over Qbar_l, hence semisimple; by Step 1, P^r is an F-stable subspace of V_r, so by eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_515 the restriction F|_{P^r} is semisimple, i.e. diagonalizable over Qbar_l. Together with the containment of Step 1 this is the right-hand side.

STEP 3 (if). Assume F(P^r) contained in P^r and F|_{P^r} diagonalizable over Qbar_l (equivalently semisimple) for every 0 <= r <= d. Fix n with 0 <= n <= 2d; for n < 0 or n > 2d we have V_n = 0 by Step 0 and there is nothing to prove. By Step 0, V is finite-dimensional Z-graded with V_n = 0 outside [0,2d], and L(V_n) is contained in V_{n+2} because L is cup product with xi in H^2; by hypothesis L^{d-n} : V_n -> V_{2d-n} is an isomorphism for every 0 <= n <= d. Hence Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_523 applies to V, L and d, and gives that the addition map direct sum_{k >= max(0,n-d)} P^{n-2k} -> V_n, (x_k) |-> sum_k L^k x_k, is an isomorphism of Q_l-vector spaces. Thus V_n = direct sum_k L^k(P^{n-2k}) is a direct sum of the subspaces L^k(P^{n-2k}); the sum is finite, since P^m = 0 for m < 0 and for m > d, so only the k with 0 <= n-2k <= d contribute.

For each such k put r = n-2k, so that 0 <= r <= d: indeed r >= 0 because n-2k >= 0, and if n <= d then r <= n <= d, while if n > d then k >= n-d and r <= n - 2(n-d) = 2d - n < d. Moreover d - r - k = d - n + k >= 0 (for n <= d this is immediate from k >= 0; for n > d it follows from k >= n-d). Hence L^{d-r} = L^{d-r-k} circ L^k, and L^{d-r} : V_r -> V_{2d-r} is an isomorphism by hypothesis; therefore L^k : V_r -> V_n is injective, and consequently L^k : P^r -> L^k(P^r) is an isomorphism of Q_l-vector spaces onto its image.

By Step 1 the subspace L^k(P^r) of V_n is stable under F and under F^{-1}, so F|_{L^k(P^r)} lies in GL. From F circ L^k = q^{mk} L^k circ F we obtain F|_{L^k(P^r)} = q^{mk} L^k circ (F|_{P^r}) circ (L^k)^{-1}, where (L^k)^{-1} denotes the inverse of the isomorphism L^k : P^r -> L^k(P^r). Since q^{mk} is a nonzero element of Q_l and F|_{P^r} is semisimple, the scalar multiple q^{mk} F|_{P^r} is semisimple (its minimal polynomial is the squarefree minimal polynomial of F|_{P^r} with the variable rescaled by q^{mk}), and conjugation by a linear isomorphism preserves semisimplicity; hence F|_{L^k(P^r)} is semisimple, i.e. diagonalizable over Qbar_l.

Thus V_n is the direct sum of finitely many F-stable subspaces, on each of which F acts semisimply. Applying eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_9 to these finitely many nonzero summands (each operator is invertible as noted above), F is semisimple on V_n, hence diagonalizable over Qbar_l. As n was arbitrary, the "if" direction holds.

Combining Steps 2 and 3 yields the asserted equivalence.

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let l != p be prime, let m>=1, and put k=overline(F_q). Let X be a smooth projective geometrically connected variety of pure dimension d>=1 over F_{q^m}. Fix a nonzero element of Q_l(1) and identify Tate twists with Q_l. Let xi in H^2_et(X_k,Q_l) be the cycle class of an F_{q^m}-rational very ample divisor, let L be cup product with xi, and let tr_X:H^{2d}_et(X_k,Q_l)->Q_l be the Poincare duality trace normalised by tr_X(cl(z))=[kappa(z):F_{q^m}]. Suppose L^{d-n}:H^n_et(X_k,Q_l)->H^{2d-n}_et(X_k,Q_l) is an isomorphism for every 0<=n<=d. For 0<=r<=d put P^r=ker(L^{d-r+1}:H^r_et(X_k,Q_l)->H^{2d-r+2}_et(X_k,Q_l)) and beta_r(x,y)=tr_X(L^{d-r}x cup y). Then beta_r restricts to a perfect pairing on P^r.
proof:
Proof. Put ℓ = l and V^n := H^n_ét(X_k, Q_ℓ) for n ∈ ℤ, with V^n = 0 for n < 0 by convention. For k ≥ 0 let L^k denote cup product with ξ^k ∈ H^{2k}_ét(X_k, Q_ℓ); thus L^0 = id, L^{k+1} = L ∘ L^k, and by associativity of the cup product, for a ∈ V^m and b ∈ V^n one has L^k a ∪ b = a ∪ L^k b = L^k(a ∪ b) whenever the degrees make sense. The hypothesis is that L^{d-n} : V^n → V^{2d-n} is an isomorphism for every integer n with 0 ≤ n ≤ d.

Step 0 (preliminaries). (0.1) Each V^n is a finite-dimensional Q_ℓ-vector space: apply lemma_45_finite_frob with base field F_{q^m} (a finite field of characteristic p), with X proper over F_{q^m}, and with K = Q_ℓ the constant sheaf on X_k equipped with its natural arithmetic Frobenius isomorphism (the algebraic closure of F_{q^m} is k). (0.2) V^n = 0 for every integer n > 2d: lemma_projective_top_degree_vanishing applied to the projective k-scheme X_k, which has pure dimension d, and to ℓ ≠ p = char(k). (0.3) The trace. By lemma_77(a) applied to X over F_{q^m}, there is an isomorphism tr : V^{2d} → Q_ℓ(−d) with tr(cl(z)) = [κ(z) : F_{q^m}] for every closed point z of X. Hence dim_{Q_ℓ} V^{2d} = 1; and for any closed point z we have tr(cl(z)) = [κ(z) : F_{q^m}] ≠ 0, so cl(z) ≠ 0 and therefore cl(z) spans V^{2d}. Consequently a Q_ℓ-linear map V^{2d} → Q_ℓ(−d) is uniquely determined by its value on cl(z). The map tr_X of the statement is Q_ℓ-valued and has the same normalisation tr_X(cl(z)) = [κ(z) : F_{q^m}]; using the fixed nonzero element of Q_ℓ(1) to identify Q_ℓ(−d) with Q_ℓ, we conclude that tr_X = tr. (0.4) By lemma_77(b), for every integer n with 0 ≤ n ≤ 2d the pairing ⟨ , ⟩_n : V^n × V^{2d−n} → Q_ℓ, ⟨a,b⟩_n := tr_X(a ∪ b), is a perfect pairing of Q_ℓ-vector spaces (i.e. both induced maps into the dual spaces are isomorphisms).

Step 1 (beta_r is a perfect pairing on V^r × V^r, for every 0 ≤ r ≤ d). Fix r with 0 ≤ r ≤ d. For x, y ∈ V^r we have L^{d−r}x ∈ V^{2d−r}, so beta_r(x,y) = tr_X(L^{d−r}x ∪ y) = ⟨L^{d−r}x, y⟩_{2d−r} is defined; note 0 ≤ 2d−r ≤ 2d, so (0.4) applies to ⟨ , ⟩_{2d−r}. By hypothesis, L^{d−r} : V^r → V^{2d−r} is an isomorphism.

Left radical. Let x ∈ V^r satisfy beta_r(x,y) = 0 for all y ∈ V^r. Then ⟨L^{d−r}x, y⟩_{2d−r} = 0 for all y ∈ V^r, i.e. the single element L^{d−r}x ∈ V^{2d−r} is orthogonal to all of V^r. Since ⟨ , ⟩_{2d−r} is perfect on V^{2d−r} × V^r, this forces L^{d−r}x = 0. Since L^{d−r} is injective, x = 0.

Right radical. Let y ∈ V^r satisfy beta_r(x,y) = 0 for all x ∈ V^r. Since L^{d−r} : V^r → V^{2d−r} is surjective, every a ∈ V^{2d−r} has the form a = L^{d−r}x with x ∈ V^r, and then ⟨a, y⟩_{2d−r} = beta_r(x,y) = 0. Thus y is orthogonal to all of V^{2d−r}, and perfectness of ⟨ , ⟩_{2d−r} gives y = 0.

Since V^r is finite-dimensional by (0.1), the vanishing of both radicals means that the maps V^r → (V^r)^*, x ↦ beta_r(x, ·) and y ↦ beta_r(·, y), are injective and hence, as dim V^r = dim (V^r)^*, are isomorphisms. Therefore beta_r is a perfect pairing on V^r × V^r.

Step 2 (primitive decomposition in degree r, for 2 ≤ r ≤ d). Claim: V^r = P^r ⊕ L(V^{r−2}). (2.1) L^{d−r+2} : V^{r−2} → V^{2d−r+2} is an isomorphism by the hypothesis applied to n = r−2 (note 0 ≤ r−2 ≤ d). (2.2) L : V^{r−2} → V^r is injective: if La = 0, then L^{d−r+2}a = L^{d−r+1}(La) = 0, so a = 0 by (2.1). (2.3) L^{d−r+1}(V^r) ⊇ L^{d−r+1}(L(V^{r−2})) = L^{d−r+2}(V^{r−2}) = V^{2d−r+2} by (2.1); hence L^{d−r+1} : V^r → V^{2d−r+2} is surjective, and its kernel is P^r by definition. (2.4) By rank–nullity and (2.1), dim V^r = dim P^r + dim V^{2d−r+2} = dim P^r + dim V^{r−2} = dim P^r + dim L(V^{r−2}). (2.5) P^r ∩ L(V^{r−2}) = 0: if Lc ∈ P^r, then 0 = L^{d−r+1}(Lc) = L^{d−r+2}c, so c = 0 by (2.1). By (2.4) and (2.5), dim(P^r + L(V^{r−2})) = dim V^r, hence V^r = P^r ⊕ L(V^{r−2}).

Step 3 (orthogonality). Let x ∈ P^r and c ∈ V^{r−2}. Then beta_r(x, Lc) = tr_X(L^{d−r}x ∪ Lc) = tr_X(L^{d−r+1}x ∪ c) = tr_X(0 ∪ c) = 0, because L^{d−r}x ∪ Lc = (L^{d−r}x ∪ ξ) ∪ c = L^{d−r+1}x ∪ c, and L^{d−r+1}x = 0 by the definition of P^r. Next, for u, v ∈ V^r, graded commutativity of the cup product gives L^{d−r}u ∪ v = (−1)^{(2d−r)r} v ∪ L^{d−r}u, and v ∪ L^{d−r}u = v ∪ ξ^{d−r} ∪ u = ξ^{d−r} ∪ v ∪ u = L^{d−r}v ∪ u (ξ has even degree); hence beta_r(u,v) = (−1)^{(2d−r)r} beta_r(v,u). Applying this with u = Lc and v = x yields beta_r(Lc, x) = (−1)^{(2d−r)r} beta_r(x, Lc) = 0. Thus P^r is orthogonal to L(V^{r−2}) with respect to beta_r on both sides.

Step 4 (restriction to P^r is perfect, for 2 ≤ r ≤ d). Let x ∈ P^r satisfy beta_r(x, p) = 0 for all p ∈ P^r. For arbitrary z ∈ V^r, write z = p + Lc with p ∈ P^r and c ∈ V^{r−2}, which is possible by Step 2. Then beta_r(x, z) = beta_r(x, p) + beta_r(x, Lc) = 0 + 0 = 0 by Step 3. Hence x lies in the left radical of beta_r on V^r, which is zero by Step 1; so x = 0. Similarly, let y ∈ P^r satisfy beta_r(p, y) = 0 for all p ∈ P^r. For z = p + Lc as above, beta_r(z, y) = beta_r(p, y) + beta_r(Lc, y) = 0 + 0 = 0 by Step 3, so y lies in the right radical of beta_r on V^r, which is zero by Step 1; so y = 0. Since P^r is finite-dimensional (it is a subspace of V^r), the vanishing of both radicals means that the restriction beta_r|_{P^r × P^r} is a perfect pairing.

Step 5 (the cases r = 0 and r = 1). P^0 = ker(L^{d+1} : V^0 → V^{2d+2}) = V^0, because V^{2d+2} = 0 by (0.2) as 2d+2 > 2d. Likewise P^1 = ker(L^d : V^1 → V^{2d+1}) = V^1, because V^{2d+1} = 0 by (0.2). Hence for r = 0 and r = 1 the restriction of beta_r to P^r × P^r is beta_r itself, which is a perfect pairing by Step 1.

Combining Step 4 (covering 2 ≤ r ≤ d) with Step 5 (covering r = 0, 1), the form beta_r restricts to a perfect pairing on P^r for every integer r with 0 ≤ r ≤ d. This is precisely the assertion of the lemma. ∎

statement: Let q=p^a be a prime power, let \(\ell\neq p\) be prime, let \(m\ge1\), and put \(k=\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). Let \(X\) be smooth projective geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d\ge2\) over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), let \(Y\subset X\) be a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor defined over \(\mathbb F_{q^m}\), smooth and geometrically connected of pure dimension \(d-1\), with closed immersion \(i:Y\hookrightarrow X\) and open complement \(j:U=X\setminus Y\hookrightarrow X\). Fix a nonzero element of \(\mathbb Q_\ell(1)\) and identify Tate twists with \(\mathbb Q_\ell\). Let \(\xi\in H^2_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) be the cycle class of \(Y\), let \(L\) be cup product with \(\xi\), and put \(P^d=\ker\bigl(L:H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d+2}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr)\). Suppose \(L^{\,d-n}:H^n_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{2d-n}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\) is an isomorphism for every \(0\le n\le d\). Then the restriction \(j^*\) restricts to an isomorphism of \(\mathbb Q_\ell[F]\)-modules \(P^d \xrightarrow{\sim} \ker\bigl[H^d_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\to H^{d-1}_{\mathrm{\acute et}}(Y_k,\mathbb Q_\ell)\bigr]\), where \(F\) is the \(q^m\)-power arithmetic Frobenius and the right-hand map is the connecting homomorphism of the Gysin sequence of \((X,Y)\).
proof:
Throughout write H^n(X)=H^n_{\mathrm{et}}(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell), and similarly H^n(Y), H^n(U). The chosen nonzero element of \mathbb Q_\ell(1) identifies every Tate twist \mathbb Q_\ell(r) with \mathbb Q_\ell; all cohomology groups below are regarded as \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces under this identification. Let F_X, F_Y, F_U denote the q^m-power arithmetic Frobenius (\mathrm{id}\times\mathrm{Spec}\,\sigma)^*, \sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, on the cohomology of X_k, Y_k, U_k respectively. Note that Y is a nonempty effective very ample Cartier divisor, hence in particular a nonempty smooth effective ample divisor of pure dimension d-1 defined over \mathbb F_{q^m}, and Y\subsetneq X because \dim Y=d-1<d=\dim X.

Preliminary remark on instantiating the cited lemmas. Several of the lemmas quoted below are stated for a variety over \mathbb F_q and the q-power Frobenius. We apply each of them with the prime power q replaced by q^m=p^{am}. Then the base field is \mathbb F_{q^m} and the corresponding Frobenius is \sigma(c)=c^{q^m}, so the hypotheses are met verbatim; this is legitimate because those lemmas are universally quantified over all prime powers. We shall not repeat this remark at every citation.

Step 1 (the Gysin sequence and its exactness). By [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_ordinary_gysin_sequence_open_complement] applied to X over \mathbb F_{q^m} and the smooth effective divisor Y of pure dimension d-1, there is a long exact sequence of \mathbb Q_\ell-vector spaces
\cdots\to H^{n-2}(Y)(-1)\xrightarrow{i_!}H^n(X)\xrightarrow{j^*}H^n(U)\xrightarrow{\partial}H^{n-1}(Y)(-1)\xrightarrow{i_!}H^{n+1}(X)\to\cdots,
where i_! is the Gysin homomorphism and \partial is the connecting homomorphism. Under the fixed identification of Tate twists with \mathbb Q_\ell this becomes an exact sequence
\cdots\to H^{n-2}(Y)\xrightarrow{i_!}H^n(X)\xrightarrow{j^*}H^n(U)\xrightarrow{\partial}H^{n-1}(Y)\xrightarrow{i_!}H^{n+1}(X)\to\cdots .
Taking n=d gives the exact fragment
H^{d-2}(Y)\xrightarrow{i_!}H^d(X)\xrightarrow{j^*}H^d(U)\xrightarrow{\partial}H^{d-1}(Y).
Exactness yields the three facts
(i) \ker\bigl(j^*:H^d(X)\to H^d(U)\bigr)=\mathrm{im}\bigl(i_!:H^{d-2}(Y)\to H^d(X)\bigr);
(ii) \ker\bigl(\partial:H^d(U)\to H^{d-1}(Y)\bigr)=\mathrm{im}\bigl(j^*:H^d(X)\to H^d(U)\bigr);
(iii) j^*\circ i_!=0 on H^{d-2}(Y).

Step 2 (the identity L=i_!\,i^* in degree d-2). The map i_! in Step 1 is the Gysin homomorphism attached to the closed immersion i:Y\hookrightarrow X (the map induced by the purity isomorphism \mathbb Q_\ell(-1)[-2]\cong i^!\mathbb Q_\ell); its standard characterisation by the projection formula is the one used in [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_439_gysin_projection_formula_divisor]. Applying that lemma with n=d-2 (which is \ge 0 since d\ge 2) and with the same fixed identification \mathbb Q_\ell(1)\cong\mathbb Q_\ell, we obtain, for every z\in H^{d-2}(X),
(2.1)  i_!(i^*z)=z\cup\xi=Lz.

Step 3 (computation of \ker j^* in degree d). Since d\ge 2 we have d-2<d-1; hence by [Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_420] applied to X_k and the nonempty effective ample Cartier divisor Y_k\subsetneq X_k, smooth of pure dimension d-1 over k, the restriction map i^*:H^{d-2}(X)\to H^{d-2}(Y) is an isomorphism. Therefore every y\in H^{d-2}(Y) is of the form y=i^*z with the unique z=(i^*)^{-1}y, and (2.1) gives i_!y=L\bigl((i^*)^{-1}y\bigr). Consequently i_!=L\circ(i^*)^{-1} as maps H^{d-2}(Y)\to H^d(X), and since (i^*)^{-1} is bijective,
\mathrm{im}\bigl(i_!:H^{d-2}(Y)\to H^d(X)\bigr)=\mathrm{im}\bigl(L:H^{d-2}(X)\to H^d(X)\bigr)=L\bigl(H^{d-2}(X)\bigr).
Combining this with Step 1(i) we obtain
(3.1)  \ker\bigl(j^*:H^d(X)\to H^d(U)\bigr)=L\bigl(H^{d-2}(X)\bigr).

Step 4 (Hard Lefschetz decomposition of H^d(X)). The hypothesis of the lemma with n=d-2 (legitimate because 0\le d-2\le d) says that L^{2}:H^{d-2}(X)\to H^{d+2}(X) is an isomorphism. In particular L:H^{d-2}(X)\to H^d(X) is injective: if Lz=0 for some z\in H^{d-2}(X), then L^2z=L(Lz)=0, and injectivity of L^2 forces z=0. Hence the hypothesis of [Spark/043be352939fa7b2/lemma_primitive_middle_decomposition_criterion] is satisfied, and its condition (ii) is exactly the isomorphism L^2 just noted; the lemma therefore yields
(4.1)  H^d(X)=P^d\oplus L\bigl(H^{d-2}(X)\bigr)=P^d\oplus\ker j^*,
the second equality by (3.1).

Step 5 (j^* maps P^d isomorphically onto \ker\partial).
(a) Well-definedness: if x\in P^d, then j^*x\in\mathrm{im}(j^*)=\ker\partial by Step 1(ii).
(b) Injectivity: if x\in P^d and j^*x=0, then x\in P^d\cap\ker j^*=0 by (4.1); hence j^*|_{P^d} is injective.
(c) Surjectivity: let u\in\ker\partial. By Step 1(ii) there exists x\in H^d(X) with j^*x=u. By (4.1) write x=x_0+Lz with x_0\in P^d and z\in H^{d-2}(X). By (2.1) we have Lz=i_!\,i^*z, and j^*\circ i_!=0 on H^{d-2}(Y) by Step 1(iii); hence j^*Lz=0. Therefore u=j^*x=j^*x_0+j^*Lz=j^*x_0 with x_0\in P^d, which proves that j^*|_{P^d} is surjective onto \ker\partial.
Thus j^*|_{P^d}:P^d\to\ker\partial is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism.

Step 6 (F-equivariance).
(a) By [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_frob_lefschetz_stable] applied with Y in the role of the very ample divisor H, we have F_X\circ L=q^m\,L\circ F_X on every H^n(X), and the subspace P^d=\ker(L:H^d(X)\to H^{d+2}(X)) is stable under F_X and F_X^{-1}. In particular F_X(P^d)\subseteq P^d.
(b) By [eoinm/edff910ca01a2397/lemma_214] applied to the morphism j:U\to X of schemes of finite type over \mathbb F_{q^m} (with q replaced by q^m as explained at the start), the pullback j^*:H^d(X)\to H^d(U) satisfies
(6.1)  j^*\circ F_X=F_U\circ j^*  on H^d(X).
(Equivalently F_U\circ j^*=j^*\circ F_X; this is the correct direction, with F_X the Frobenius on the target X and F_U the Frobenius on the source U of j.)
(c) Consequently, for x\in P^d we have F_U(j^*x)=j^*(F_Xx) by (6.1), and F_Xx\in P^d by (a); hence F_U(j^*x)\in j^*(P^d)=\ker\partial. Therefore \ker\partial is F_U-stable, and j^*|_{P^d} intertwines F_X|_{P^d} with F_U|_{\ker\partial}, i.e. j^*\circ F_X=F_U\circ j^* on P^d.

Conclusion. By Step 5, j^*|_{P^d}:P^d\to\ker\bigl(\partial:H^d(U)\to H^{d-1}(Y)\bigr) is a \mathbb Q_\ell-linear isomorphism, and by Step 6 it is F-equivariant, i.e. j^*\circ F_X=F_U\circ j^* on P^d. Hence it is an isomorphism of \mathbb Q_\ell[F]-modules, where F acts as F_X on P^d\subseteq H^d(X_k,\mathbb Q_\ell) and as F_U on \ker\partial\subseteq H^d(U_k,\mathbb Q_\ell). This is precisely the assertion of the lemma.
